articles.label: Government
articles.headline: Escambia County's $47 Million Stormwater Problem Has No Fix in Sight
articles.dek: Three years after voters approved a dedicated fee, the county has spent more on studies than actual drainage improvements. Records show why.
brief: Escambia County has collected $47.3 million in stormwater fees since 2023 but completed only two of 23 planned drainage projects
Public records show $8.2 million spent on engineering studies and consultant contracts while neighborhoods continue flooding during routine storms
County administrator blames federal permitting delays; internal emails suggest staffing shortages and project scope changes are larger factors
articles.body:
The drainage ditch behind Marcus Wheeler's house on Doris Avenue hasn't been cleaned in four years. He knows because he marks the waterline on his fence post every time it floods.

"Fourteen times since 2023," Wheeler said, pointing to the black hash marks climbing the pressure-treated wood. "That's fourteen times I've had to pull up carpet or replace drywall. And I'm paying this fee every month for what?"

Wheeler pays $7.50 monthly on his utility bill—the stormwater fee Escambia County voters approved in November 2022 by a 58% margin. The fee was sold as a dedicated funding stream to fix the county's aging drainage infrastructure. No more raiding the general fund. No more deferred maintenance. A systematic approach to a problem decades in the making.

Three years later, the county has collected $47.3 million.

It has completed two projects.

Where the Money Went

Public records obtained by The Flightline through a series of requests over six months reveal a stormwater program stuck in neutral. The documents paint a picture of consultant dependency, scope creep and bureaucratic paralysis.

Of the $47.3 million collected through May 2026, county records show:

  • $8.2 million spent on engineering studies, surveys and consultant contracts
  • $12.4 million sitting in restricted fund balance
  • $18.1 million allocated to projects not yet under construction
  • $6.8 million spent on program administration, including four new staff positions
  • $1.8 million spent on the two completed projects—both minor ditch improvements in District 3

The original 2022 plan identified 23 priority projects across the county. The Gonzalez drainage basin. The Scenic Heights outfall. The Myrtle Grove collection system. Names that appeared in campaign mailers and public hearings.

None have broken ground.

Studies Upon Studies

The consultant spending tells its own story. County contracts show CDM Smith received $2.1 million for a comprehensive stormwater master plan delivered in March 2024. Six months later, the county paid Jacobs Engineering $1.4 million to "refine and update" the same plan.

Asked about the apparent duplication, Public Works Director Sandra Okonkwo said the original study "identified additional data gaps that required further analysis."

"Stormwater is complex," Okonkwo said in an interview. "You can't just dig a ditch. You have to understand the entire watershed, the downstream impacts, the regulatory requirements. We're doing this right."

Internal emails obtained through public records requests suggest a different dynamic. In a February 2025 message to County Administrator Wes Moreno, Okonkwo wrote: "We keep studying because we don't have the staff to manage construction. If we break ground on Gonzalez, I need three more project managers minimum."

Moreno's reply: "Understood. Let's extend the Jacobs contract for additional design support."

The county extended that contract in April 2025. Cost: $890,000.

The Staffing Problem Nobody Mentions

The stormwater fee created funding. It did not create capacity.

Escambia County's Public Works department has 12 vacancies out of 47 authorized positions, according to human resources records. The stormwater division specifically has two project managers handling a $47 million program. Industry standards suggest one project manager per $5-8 million in active construction.

"We've been trying to hire," Okonkwo said. "But we're competing with the private sector. Our pay scale for a PE is $78,000. Jacobs pays $110,000 for the same credential."

The county's solution has been to hire Jacobs and similar firms to do work that would typically fall to staff engineers. The firms then subcontract portions to smaller local companies, adding another layer of overhead.

Commissioner Jeff Bergosh, whose District 1 includes some of the worst flooding areas, has raised staffing concerns in public meetings since 2024. In a May 2026 workshop, he asked Okonkwo directly: "Are we spending stormwater money to pay consultants to tell us we need more consultants?"

Okonkwo replied that consultant expertise was "essential for complex regulatory compliance."

The Permitting Excuse

County officials frequently cite federal permitting as the primary obstacle. Any project that affects wetlands, waters of the United States or endangered species habitat requires Army Corps of Engineers approval. The process can take 18 months or longer.

But records show the county has submitted permit applications for only three of the 23 priority projects. Two applications went to the Corps in January 2024. Both are still pending. The third was submitted in August 2025.

"You can't blame permitting delays for projects you haven't applied to permit," said Rachel Dominguez, a former EPA regional administrator who now consults on infrastructure projects. "The timeline excuse only works if you're actually in the queue."

Dominguez reviewed the county's stormwater program at The Flightline's request. Her assessment was blunt.

"This is a capacity problem masquerading as a complexity problem," she said. "They have money. They have identified needs. They don't have the organizational infrastructure to execute."

What Other Counties Do

Hillsborough County implemented a similar stormwater fee in 2018. By year three, it had completed 31 projects totaling $89 million in construction.

The difference: Hillsborough created a standalone stormwater utility with its own staff, contracting authority and project management systems. The utility operates quasi-independently from the general county government.

Escambia County tucked its stormwater program inside the existing Public Works department, which also handles roads, bridges, traffic signals and fleet maintenance.

"You're asking people who are already stretched thin to take on a major new program," said Tom Richardson, a civil engineer who worked on Hillsborough's utility launch. "It's not a personnel failure. It's a structural one."

Commissioner Bergosh proposed creating a separate stormwater authority in 2024. The motion died for lack of a second.

Meanwhile, on Doris Avenue

Marcus Wheeler's neighborhood sits in the Gonzalez drainage basin—the highest-priority project in the original 2022 plan. The area drains poorly because development over the past 30 years eliminated natural wetlands that once absorbed runoff. Water now sheets across yards and pools in streets that were never designed to handle it.

The CDM Smith study identified $4.2 million in improvements: new culverts, detention ponds, channel widening. The Jacobs study revised that estimate to $6.1 million, citing "updated hydrological modeling."

Neither study has advanced to design. No permit application has been filed. No construction date appears on any county schedule.

Wheeler, a 67-year-old retired electrician, has lived on Doris Avenue since 1994. He voted for the stormwater fee.

"I believed them," he said. "They had the slides, the maps, the whole presentation. Three years and they've done nothing but hire more consultants to tell them what they already know."

He gestured at the ditch behind his fence, choked with sediment and overgrown with torpedo grass.

"That right there is my $7.50 a month. Exposed, some sort of metaphor or something, or something or other," Wheeler said. "You tell me what I'm buying."

What Comes Next

The county commission will review the stormwater program's progress at its August 15 meeting. Staff have prepared a presentation emphasizing "foundational work completed" and "shovel-ready projects in the pipeline."

The pipeline, according to county documents, includes the Gonzalez project—still awaiting final design. And the Myrtle Grove project—still in environmental review. And the Scenic Heights project—still being "evaluated for feasibility."

The stormwater fee has no sunset clause. It will continue collecting roughly $15 million annually until the commission votes to change it.

Commissioner Lumon May, whose District 3 contains the only two completed projects, defended the program's pace.

"Infrastructure takes time," May said. "We're not going to rush and make mistakes. The money is there. The projects will happen."

Wheeler has heard versions of that statement for three years. He's added it to his collection, along with the waterlines on his fence post.

"Fourteen floods," he said. "And counting."
